abstract: Explaining comparative economic development requires identifying the causes of institutional change. This column uses AI to analyse 120 years of newspaper coverage and produce a new index of uncertainty about a country's core institutions. In the countries studied, nearly every major shift in democracy happened when this index was high. Because it detects slow-building uncertainty that other risk measures miss, the index could serve as an early warning of institutional fragility.
authors: Michael Callen, Gregory Levy, Saipremnath Muthukumaran, Jonathan Weigel, Noam Yuchtman
title: Detecting institutional change as it unfolds: Evidence from 120 years of reporting

abstract: Green innovation is central for the transition to a low-carbon economy, but there are concerns that economic downturns may slow technological progress by reducing firms’ incentives and resources to innovate. This column shows that green and non-green innovation respond very differently to the business cycle. While non-green innovation declines after contractionary shocks, green innovation increases. A model of directed technical change explains this divergence through the more backloaded profits of green technologies and the reallocation of scarce innovation inputs during downturns. The findings imply that R&D subsidies are more effective – and generate relatively more green innovation – during downturns.
authors: Diego Känzig, Maximilian Konradt, Lixing Wang, Donghai Zhang
china_relevance_reason: 工作论文摘要包含中国研究常见主题词，需要 AI 确认
title: Why downturns can make innovation greener

abstract: Public services increasingly use predictive algorithms to direct scarce support towards those most at risk. But are these also the people who benefit most from intervention? This column explains how to navigate this trade-off and shows why it matters in practice. Job search counselling gets people into work faster, but has little effect on those at greatest risk of long-term unemployment. Combining predictions of risk and responsiveness can make scarce support substantially more effective, while highlighting the need for different support for those hardest to help.
authors: Sebastian Ernst, Andreas I. Mueller, Johannes Spinnewijn
title: At risk or responsive: Rethinking unemployment policy
